articles.headline: OFAC Removes Designation Related to Venezuela Sanctions Program
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a Venezuela-related designation removal on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a change in the sanctions landscape concerning individuals or entities previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.

While the specific details of the removed designation were not immediately released, such removals typically follow a review of the circumstances that led to the initial designation, including changes in behavior or ownership, or a determination that the designation no longer serves U.S. foreign policy objectives.

This removal could signal a potential shift in the broader U.S. approach to Venezuela, or it may be a targeted action reflecting individual compliance or a reassessment of specific entities within the existing sanctions framework.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions are part of ongoing U.S. efforts to disrupt illicit financial networks that support drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally.

These designations typically involve freezing assets under U.S. jurisdiction and prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties. The move underscores the U.S. commitment to combating these threats through financial sanctions.

The specific individuals and entities targeted were not immediately detailed in the announcement, but such designations aim to isolate them from the international financial system and limit their ability to conduct illicit operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues International Criminal Court Designation and General Licenses, Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on October 9, 2026, including a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC), the issuance of new general licenses, and the removal of a Burma-related designation. This multifaceted announcement reflects varied U.S. foreign policy objectives and ongoing adjustments to sanctions programs.

The ICC designation signals U.S. concerns regarding the court's actions or jurisdiction, while the new general licenses aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, likely to facilitate humanitarian aid or other permitted activities. Concurrently, the removal of a Burma-related designation suggests a reassessment of specific entities or a response to developments within Burma.

These actions collectively demonstrate OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, utilizing both restrictive measures and facilitative authorizations to achieve strategic goals across different geopolitical contexts.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This action provides authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the extensive sanctions regime targeting Russia.

General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to carve out specific activities from broader sanctions, often to facilitate humanitarian efforts, ensure the flow of certain goods or services, or to align with allied policies.
The specific scope of this new General License will be detailed in the official publication, and it is crucial for U.S. persons and entities to review its provisions carefully to ensure compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses for Iran and Russia
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, alongside the issuance of a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These actions underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on Iran while also adjusting parameters for engagement with both Iran and Russia.

The Iran-related designations aim to further disrupt networks supporting the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities. Concurrently, the new Iran-related General License may permit certain transactions, potentially for humanitarian purposes or to facilitate specific types of trade not deemed sanctionable.

The amended Russia-related General License indicates a refinement of existing authorizations, likely in response to evolving geopolitical circumstances or to address specific compliance challenges faced by businesses operating under the Russia sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ, Announces Designations Removals and Updates
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an Iran-related Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 5, 2026. This alert warns foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that they could be targeted at any time without advance notification if they continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions.

OFAC also amended Iran-related FAQ 156, removing language that previously indicated OFAC would generally contact an FFI before making a finding of sanctionable activity. This change signals a more aggressive enforcement posture, emphasizing that FFIs with exposure to Iranian banks should promptly review their relationships.

In addition to the Iran-focused guidance, OFAC announced designations removals and updates, indicating ongoing adjustments to its various sanctions lists. These removals and updates reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions, responding to changes in circumstances or policy objectives.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting or engaging in acts of terrorism, aiming to disrupt their financial networks and operations.

These actions are a critical component of the U.S. government's strategy to combat global terrorism by cutting off access to financial resources. Designated parties face asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.

The specific details of the designated individuals and entities were not immediately available, but such measures are intended to increase pressure on terrorist organizations and their facilitators worldwide.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Iran-Related Designations and Updates, Issues Determination and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and designations updates on October 1, 2026. These actions are part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast,' launched by OFAC on August 24, 2026, to cut off financial resources supporting the Iranian regime.

Concurrently, OFAC issued a Transnational Criminal Organizations Designation, a new Iran-related Determination, and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question. These measures collectively aim to strengthen the existing sanctions framework against Iran and address evolving threats.

The amended FAQ and new determination provide further clarity and guidance on compliance obligations, reflecting the U.S. government's commitment to a robust and adaptive sanctions policy against Iran.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations, Removes Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations on September 30, 2026. This action reinforces the U.S. commitment to combating these illicit networks by imposing financial restrictions.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also announced the removal of designations related to Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya. These removals suggest a reassessment of the entities or individuals previously sanctioned under these programs, potentially due to changed circumstances or policy shifts.
These combined actions highlight OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, simultaneously imposing new restrictions where threats persist and adjusting existing measures as conditions evolve.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 Over Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to a settlement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $11,662,930. This settlement resolves apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred due to a combination of technical and human errors, such as channeling correspondent banking payments through blocked banks, allowing designated individuals to make payments and withdraw funds due to poor sanctions alert calibration, and failing to promptly update watchlists.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement amount reflects no reduction to the base penalty, including no mitigation for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $175,015. This settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

Details of the specific violations were not immediately available, but such settlements typically involve companies that have engaged in transactions or activities that contravene U.S. sanctions programs.
The resolution with OFAC underscores the importance of robust compliance programs for companies operating internationally, particularly those involved in logistics and trade.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations

The specific nature of the individual's violations was not detailed in the public announcement, but OFAC civil penalties against individuals often relate to unauthorized transactions with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions.
This penalty serves as a reminder that sanctions compliance is not solely a corporate responsibility but extends to individuals who may engage in prohibited activities.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This penalty is the largest in OCC history and comes nearly two years after the bank signed a cease-and-desist order in December 2024 to address its deficient BSA/AML compliance program.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program remained deficient and ineffective, with its transaction monitoring system failing to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This led to the bank filing a large number of late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars.

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould stated that the bank's poor response to its BSA deficiencies was unacceptable, emphasizing that the egregious and continued BSA violations warranted the largest civil money penalty ever assessed against a bank. The OCC's action was taken in coordination with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), which assessed a $1.2 billion fine against Bank of America, crediting the OCC's penalty.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / U.S. Treasury

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express for BSA/AML Program Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program. The OCC determined that the bank failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations.

Deficiencies in the bank's BSA/AML program included inadequate resources, staff without sufficient expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and insufficient BSA/AML training for employees and directors. The OCC found that American Express failed to tailor its BSA/AML risk assessment to its business activities, focusing insufficiently on the risks in its more dominant credit and charge card products.

These failures contributed to the bank's inability to timely identify, evaluate, and sufficiently report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade. Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould emphasized that banks of American Express's size and complexity must devote sufficient resources to ensure compliance with laws designed to detect and prevent money laundering.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
